title: A castle of crystal (Interior Castle, 1)
hookLine: the soul is a castle with many rooms and God at the center; the door is prayer

cards: Spain, 1577. An aging nun with a head full of noise, she says, is ordered by her superiors to write a book about prayer. She doesn't want to.
She has convents to run, letters to answer, a reform to hold together. She asks God what to write. And, as she tells it, while she is praying, a picture comes to her.
The soul is a castle, made of diamond, or of very clear crystal. For the next eight days, this part of the path walks through it, room by room. Today, the front door.

teach.h: THE SOUL IS A CASTLE OF CRYSTAL.
teach.b: The nun is Teresa of Ávila, a Carmelite, later a saint and a Doctor of the Church. The book is The Interior Castle; in Spanish, Las Moradas, the dwelling places. First, the castle.
It glows, clear as crystal, with many rooms, some above, some below, some to the sides. Teresa points to Jesus's own words, in the Douay-Rheims: "In my Father's house there are many mansions."
If heaven has many rooms, she says, so does a human soul.
Second, the center. In the very middle of the castle is the main room, and there God lives. Not far off in the sky.
Inside. The soul's beauty, Teresa says, is so great you can hardly imagine it, and yet many souls never go in. They stay out in the courtyard.
Her answer is simple: the door of the castle is prayer and reflection. Not a feeling. Not being good enough.
Just turning toward God, even clumsily, even a little. Fourth, the first rooms. People who've just come in still carry a lot from outside, she says: worries, business, pride.
She pictures snakes and other vermin slipping in with them, keeping them from seeing the light. The light from the center shines the whole time; they just can't see it yet.
Her advice for these first rooms is humility: get to know yourself honestly, without panic.

teach.h: IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE THERE ARE MANY MANSIONS.
teach.b: The castle has seven sets of rooms in all, taken one at a time.

how: Many Catholics read Teresa of Ávila's Interior Castle slowly, often with a spiritual director or a prayer group, as a map of how a life of prayer grows from the first rooms toward the center.

o: Teresa's picture of the soul as rooms with God at the center
a real Spanish castle where Teresa lived as a nun
a fortress of rules that keeps sin out of the soul

games.q: what's inside the castle — tap the pairs.

s: in Teresa's castle, God lives far outside, on a hill
God lives at the very center of the castle, inside the soul.
Teresa points to Jesus's words about many rooms
"in my Father's house there are many mansions."
the light at the center switches on once you're good enough
it's shining the whole time; the people in the first rooms just can't see it yet.

games.q: you're standing outside a crystal castle, and you've been told God lives at its center. how do you get in?
o: go through the door: prayer and reflection.
wait for someone to carry you in.
games.why: Teresa says the door of the castle is prayer and reflection, even clumsy, even a little.

practice: Close your eyes and picture a clear, bright castle, with you standing just inside the door.
Notice what came in with you, a worry, a grudge, a to-do list, without fighting it, then look toward the center, where the light comes from.
If you pray, simply say, here I am; if you don't, rest in the picture of a light that was already on.

wordCard.voice: Interior Castle. Teresa of Ávila's book that pictures the soul as many rooms, God at the center, and prayer as the door. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the door is prayer. The light inside was on before you knocked. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: In my Father's house there are many mansions
